title: The Inquisition, honestly
hookLine: church courts that used coercion and handed people to execution; John Paul II asked forgiveness

lines: A SUNDAY IN LENT, SAINT PETER'S.
SINS IN THE SERVICE OF TRUTH.
cards: A Sunday in Lent, in Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome. Pope John Paul II stands before a crucifix.
One after another, cardinals step forward and name sins committed by members of the Church, and after each one the pope asks God's forgiveness.

One confession is for sins committed in the service of truth: intolerance, and force used against others in the name of faith. The cardinal who reads it leads the Vatican office that grew out of the old Roman Inquisition.
Today, the hardest part of the Dominican story, honestly.

teach.b: You met inquisitions in passing on day eight hundred forty-five. Inquisition comes from the Latin inquisitio, an inquiry, a legal investigation. It wasn't one court.
In medieval Europe, popes appointed inquisitors to investigate heresy, among them friars, Dominicans and Franciscans.
Later came the Spanish Inquisition, run under the Spanish crown, which pursued people whose families had converted from Judaism or Islam and who were suspected of keeping their old faith in secret.

teach.h: COERCION, AND HANDING PEOPLE OVER TO DIE.
teach.b: The courts questioned people. They used coercion, and at times torture. When someone was judged a heretic and wouldn't recant, the court handed them over to the civil authorities, who put them to death.
The Church didn't light the fire, but it handed the person to the ones who did. Historians argue about the numbers, and popular stories sometimes inflate them.
That doesn't change the core: the same order that preached veritas sometimes served this. So what does the Gospel say about force?

teach.h: JESUS REBUKES THE CALL FOR FIRE.
teach.b: When a Samaritan village refuses to welcome Jesus, James and John offer to call down fire from heaven. Luke says Jesus turns and rebukes them, and they go on to another village.

teach.h: PUT UP AGAIN THY SWORD INTO ITS PLACE.
teach.b: And on the night he's arrested, when a disciple draws a sword, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Put up again thy sword into its place." So the confession in Saint Peter's matters.
The Church said, in public, that people who believed they were serving the truth did it with force, and that this was sin. It wasn't explained away. Forgiveness was asked.

how: The Catholic Church has publicly confessed sins committed by its members in the use of force in the service of faith, notably in a Day of Pardon liturgy led by John Paul II; Catholics pray for the dead, including victims of religious violence, at Mass and with prayers such as 'Eternal rest'.

p: wanted fire on a Samaritan village
sins in the service of truth

s: the Inquisition was one court that never changed
there were medieval inquisitors, the Spanish Inquisition under the crown, and the Roman Inquisition.
the Church courts handed condemned people to civil authorities to be put to death
the Church didn't light the fire, but it handed the person to the ones who did.
the Church has never said anything about it in public
at a Lenten liturgy in Saint Peter's, John Paul II asked forgiveness for sins committed in the service of truth.

games.q: a Samaritan village refuses to welcome Jesus. James and John offer to call down fire from heaven on it. what does Jesus do?
o: rebuke them, and go on to another village.
go back and argue with the villagers.
games.why: Luke says he turned and rebuked them, and they went on to another village. no fire.

practice: Bring to mind the people who stood before those courts, whose names we will never know, Jews and Muslims and their descendants, people judged heretics, and then everyone, of any faith or none, hurt or killed by someone acting in the name of God.
Just hold them in silence. If you pray, you can say, "Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord," the Church's old prayer for the dead, and if not, let the quiet be your respect.

wordCard.voice: Inquisition. Church courts that investigated heresy, used coercion, and handed people over to be executed; a history the Church has publicly asked forgiveness for. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: an inquiry, a legal investigation. the root of the word Inquisition.

carryVoice: Your line: forgiveness asked. Named out loud, before a crucifix, and not explained away. Rest well.
